title: Life on a research ship
text:
Dr Marta Lis is a marine biologist. Every year she spends three months on a research ship in the Atlantic Ocean, studying whales. We talked to her during a short break at home in Gdynia.

What exactly do you do on the ship?
We follow groups of whales and record the sounds they make. Whales "talk" to each other, and we want to understand how and why. We also count them and take small skin samples to check if they are healthy.

What is a normal day like?
There's no normal day! It depends on the weather and on the whales. Sometimes we work from sunrise until midnight because a group of whales is near the ship. Other days the sea is too rough and we stay inside, analysing data on our computers.

What's the hardest thing about living on a ship?
Being far from my family. My daughter is eight, and three months is a long time for her. We have video calls when the internet works, which isn't very often. Also, the ship is small – there are twenty people, and you can't escape from anyone!

Do you ever get seasick?
Yes, during the first few days of every trip. It's awful. But after that my body gets used to it.

What has been your most exciting moment?
Two years ago, a young humpback whale swam right next to our small boat and stayed with us for almost an hour. It looked at us with its huge eye. I'll never forget it.

Are whales in danger?
Some species are. The biggest problems are noise from ships, plastic in the ocean and fishing nets. The good news is that some populations are growing again, thanks to protection. So there is hope.
